utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam Registrar, and good morning, everybody. Could you kindly call the case, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor v. Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, ma'am. All the accused are here. From the Defence teams, I notice the absence of Mr. Josse, Mr. Bourgon and Mr. Meek. The Prosecution, Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Thayer. I understand there are a couple of preliminaries that you wish to address, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone. Just a brief alert to the Chambers concerning the witness scheduling for the remainder of the week. I'm not sure the extent to which the Bench has been apprised of the picayune details of our witness scheduling. We have been working very hard to get PW-151 here from the third country in which he is currently residing. Weeks and weeks and weeks ago, we had made arrangements to have him here prior to this past weekend to begin testifying first thing this week. We advised my learned friends last week or the week before that the third country and Dutch authorities had changed that schedule. We scrambled and managed to get the current witness here earlier to fill that gap. We were then informed that it would be even later than we thought, that PW-151 would be made available by the authorities here. We again scrambled to fill that gap. So he will not be beginning his testimony until this Friday. That's the absolute earliest we believe we can have him ready. He will not arrive, we are now told, until this evening. And with the morning court schedule that we're on, we believe the earliest we could have him ready to go would be Friday, and we will have him ready to Friday. However, given the accelerated schedule already of this week, and the Court's seen, I think, some of the results of that, we may have a gap emerging tomorrow following the current witness. With the cross-examination time estimates that we'd had and, frankly, some of the direct examination time estimates we'd had, we thought we would be very comfortably able to fill the week up to Witness 151 on Friday. As of the way things stand now, it doesn't look like we're going to be able to do that. We may have, therefore, a possibly two- or three-hour gap erupting tomorrow. We are trying to find something productive to do in that time. One of the ideas we had was to clean up some of the odds and ends, exhibits issues that have been hanging fire for a little while; for example, the statement of the accused Pandurevic, which I don't believe has been fully resolved. That is something that might be able to fill some time. Other than that, we are currently without any witnesses that we can bring in any quicker just because of the visa issues that we face bringing people here from out of the country. So we wanted to alert the Court to this problem. The other possibility that we have, and I think Mr. McCloskey alluded to this yesterday, was we are scrambling to make an investigator available tomorrow to testify concerning the acquisition of the Drina Corps collection, how that came into our possession, how that was discovered, basically to explain that. That was an issue that arose yesterday. We believe that we can have an investigator ready to go as well on that issue. And if, for no other testimony than his direct, we think that that would be a productive potential use of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, Mr. Thayer. Does any one of the Defence counsel wish to address this matter, this issue? None. Okay. Anything further? Anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. I think we'll play it by ear, because for the time being you still have not finished your examination-in-chief. You asked for two hours, and at least on paper we have a request for four and a half hours of cross-examination. So we might end up, as you say, with a gap, or you never know, we might fill the time that we have up to tomorrow completely. So let's wait and see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, sir, Mr. Djuric.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome back. I hope you had a good rest. Today, we are going to continue with your testimony. Mr. Thayer will proceed with his examination-in-chief. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We left off yesterday with you telling us, I believe, that you estimated you had perhaps 70 men with you at your accommodation in the village near Bratunac, where you were accommodated in a school. This was on July 11th. And my first question for you is: Did you receive any order or instruction from Mr. Jevic later that day on the 11th as to what your assignment would be the next day?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Jevic told me that the following day, on the 12th, we would be having a police assignment, a police job, to go to Potocari, where a larger group of civilians from Srebrenica were supposed to gather, and our task was to protect those civilians, to prevent any other contacts, other groups, civilians or others, with these civilians from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did Mr. Jevic tell you what, if anything, was to become or happen to those civilians gathering in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He just told me that the politics will do their job and that those civilians would most probably be transported to the Tuzla area.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall where you were when Mr. Jevic was explaining this to you?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we talked about this assignment, I was at the school where the unit was billeted.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you know where Mr. Jevic had been spending his time during this period on the 11th?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't following Mr. Jevic. I don't know where he went, but he was absent quite a lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when he was actually in Bratunac, do you know where he was based or spending his time when he was in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where he was staying. I assume that he went to the police station quite frequently, since the headquarters was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you know from whom Mr. Jevic was receiving his information?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who he received his information from, but if it was along the line of the command and following the logic of things, I assume that it was from Mr. Borovcanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, who was the overall Special Police Brigade commander on the ground at that time in that area?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the Special Police Brigade, the person of the highest rank was Mr. Borovcanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, I want to take you to the next day, the 12th of July. Can you tell the Trial Chamber what you did that day, from the beginning, just step by step?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 12th of July, in the morning, we moved as a unit. We were taken to the check-point, to the line of separation, earlier, and I could tell by the buildings there that it used to be the line of separation there. That's where we lined up the unit, and then we set off in the direction of Potocari. We passed a UN check-point as we were in the column, and then we came to a kind of broader area, a kind of clearing which made it possible to place the unit on the left and the right side. The terrain allowed for that. We were in a kind of semi-combat position, and I was moving along the main road throughout that time. Mr. Jevic suggested to me that that area -- he assumed that the area was clear, in the sense that the Army of Republika Srpska had passed there, that there were probably no other formations there, and that this was just a routine matter to go through it just to make sure that somebody wasn't remaining behind or had been left behind. Then we continued, and then when we came to the place where the UN was located, the left flank bypassed that facility. I remember then that one of the unit members told me that there was something up there that could be seen, that there was some houses that were burned there, that you could still see the smoke. And I explained the evening before that, more or less, what they were supposed to do, how to do it, what police jobs were in front of us, that it was more or less what we had trained for. So I recall that one of the unit members asked me, "Well, all right, we're all going in a column and you are going along the road, the street," and I said, "Yes. I learned how to move a long time ago, and you are learning it now." So that, in itself, indicates that I was sure that there was nobody there. Then we -- actually, the left flank bypassed the UN base. The rest of the guys came up to that area where the civilians were gathered, and we saw some UN members there. I don't know exactly how many of them there were there, but the number kept changing. Some were coming and then some were leaving, so I don't remember how many of them were there. Then, by some kind of logic and based on experience in police work, when we come out into the field we would usually get in touch with all the persons who we find in the field, so that is why we got in touch with the members of the UN who happened to be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let me just ask you a couple of brief follow-up questions. You described, first, before you entered Potocari, passing through a UN check-point. Do you remember whether that check-point had any particular name?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I don't remember. I don't know. I was never there before, so just passing by didn't really mean anything to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you refer to your left flank bypassing the UN facility, do you mean that the left flank basically went around the UN compound?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they went around it, but we didn't leave people to surround the base. But finally, when we all met up, some members were by the base of the UN, and the rest I deployed around the civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And let's talk about the civilians for a moment, sir. Can you describe the civilians that you saw, in terms of the numbers and how they appeared to you at that time?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really couldn't estimate how many there were because these civilians kept moving around. They were going left and right, they were agitated, so I really don't have any idea how many of them there were. But new groups of civilians kept arriving, so the number was increasing, but basically all the civilians looked tired, frightened. They were crying. There were a lot of children. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you made contact with some of the UN soldiers there, can you tell the Trial Chamber who you made contact with, in particular, if anyone?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember and I recognised him in photographers, a young officer, blonde, tall, very well built, corpulent, although it was a bit unusual that in the uniform he was moving around in, it was a bit unusual for me that he was wearing short trousers, shorts, and a T-shirt, so this is not something that is standard in our -- among our troops. But he seemed to be some kind of person that was responsible.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall this soldier's rank or name?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he was a lieutenant. The names come a bit hard to me. Maybe van Duijn or something like that. I don't know. And I recognised that name in later conversations with the investigators. At the time, I didn't remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, can you describe where you physically deployed your 1st Company members at this time?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people who were with me I deployed around the civilians to protect them, so nobody could approach them, and there was a smaller group there with me right next to the civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: At some point after you reached the UN base, did you see Mr. Jevic?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Jevic came several times there. We had direct contact perhaps two or three times. If I needed something, we would communicate by radio. I didn't pay attention to how many times Mr. Jevic came, if he came or not. He had his duties, his tasks, that I didn't know about, so I had no need to look -- or control him or to look for him. We saw each other two or three times. I can say that those times were maybe some form of control. Everything else was just in passing, just like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall what Mr. Jevic's radio code-name was, sir?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Jevic's code was Staljin.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what was your code-name, sir?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My code was Javor. These were code-names that we had from the beginning, and they are something that is easy to remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And at some point that day, did you see General Mladic arrive?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from what I can recall, he was there twice right next to us. At one point, I think he came with his escort, with some people. He talked with the civilians, explaining something about transport, about -- but I really wasn't paying attention to what Mr. Mladic was talking about with the civilians. I wasn't really noticing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So what happened next, sir?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the transport began, the first vehicles appeared, and then when the first vehicles appeared the civilians were kind of frightened. They wanted to go, they didn't want to go. There was a dose of fear, I assume. However, they did go. And in the beginning, as I said, it was a bit fearful, but then when they saw that people were going in, that they were leaving, that things were proceeding in a kind of normal manner, then they went. But then we encountered other problems, and these problems were when one or two vehicles would arrive, regardless of what kind of vehicles they were, buses, trucks or some other type of vehicles, then there was a problem how to stop and how to control them from all leaving at the same time, because it wasn't possible. There wasn't enough vehicles. Then the Dutch soldiers, together with some of my men, tried, in a way, to calm them down, to control them, and at some point we were forming police cordons, we were holding hands and trying to kind of direct that crowd of people who were all practically trying to get on to one bus. That's more or less what happened. About this transport, if you want me to tell you more, it's perhaps important to say that sometimes there would be a lull, there would be no vehicles, and then five or six or ten would come in one go. I don't remember the exact numbers, but a large number of vehicles would arrive, and then we would respond trying to help people board.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, physically, sir, where were you located, if you can just generally describe where in relation, for example, to the actual UN compound you were working that day?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the first time in my life I was there, and I cannot really give you a layout of structures, but I remember the trees, and as the civilians were arriving there was a shade under the trees, and we were all standing there. And I remember that was not close to the entrance to the UN base.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So can you describe what you, yourself, were doing during this process, you personally?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there by the civilians all the time, and I was almost all the time in contact with this UN lieutenant. I simply didn't budge. That was my post, that was my assignment. I was there all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall seeing Mr. Jevic participating in the transportations in any way that day?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't come or participate in any way in the location where we were situated. Whether he was doing something elsewhere, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And were there any VRS soldiers, sir, participating in this process where you were, from what you remember?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the spot where I was just next to the civilians, the people who were coming were probably involved in organising the transport. There would be one or two men, together with the driver. They would help the buses or trucks turn around. These men would step off and direct the buses. But if you mean if there were any military units, no, there were only those individuals who arrived together with the vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you refer to individuals who arrived with the vehicles, are you referring to men who were in uniform, from what you saw?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The greatest number of them was in uniform. A few were in civilian clothing, but those were drivers.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And where you were, sir, do you recall whether there were any Serb civilians participating in this process?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Civilians in civilian clothing. I don't remember any.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you've alluded to this a little bit, sir, but can you describe, from where you were, what you recall any Dutch soldiers doing during this process?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about that group around the lieutenant. They were doing approximately the same thing as we. They were around the civilians, and as required they would streamline the civilians towards the buses. If a larger convoy arrived, it would remain parked just in front of us for a while, while the civilians boarded. Some of them helped the civilians board. There were a lot of women who had a lot of children with them and a lot of luggage, and they would help them get in. They would be especially needed if a truck had to be boarded, because it's not easy to climb onto a truck. But that's all that was happening in front of us. I really have no idea what was going on somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: How much time would you estimate that you spent at that particular location on July 12th, sir?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that day, until the last vehicles arrived, that was late afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So to the best of your recollection, what time did the transportation stop on the 12th of July, sir?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact time to the hour, but I know it was late afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So what did you do after the transportations ended that day?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We went again to our base, to that school where we were accommodated.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And at some point did you receive an order regarding redeploying the 1st Company men that were with you?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Jevic came to our base and said there was a shortage of policemen and it would be a good idea if we could help out, to cover part of the road from Bratunac to Konjevic Polje, because it was suspected that groups of Muslims from Srebrenica were not in Potocari, that they could be hiding there and could try to enter the town, so it would be a good idea to gather as many men as we could, in view of the fact that they had worked all day, to cover that road. So I picked the men who were in Potocari earlier that day but who did not do anything special, and I assigned them to be deployed along the road. I can't remember whether there was someone from the local police with me, but I know that we went somewhere from the outer populated part of Bratunac, and then at certain intervals I would deploy two or three men along the road, but not right next to the road because there was a lot of traffic. We were either further up or below the road, depending on the terrain.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall approximately how far along the road or approximately to what village on the night of the 12th you deployed your 1st Company men?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the names of these places from some earlier situations, but I was only able to really locate them later, when I was shown maps by investigators. I couldn't really say, after all that had happened the previous day, with any certainly where exactly my men were and how many there were in a group. But when the investigators showed me the map and when I tried to mark the map, I saw Glogova, and I remembered that place name, and I also remembered that we didn't enter that place. So we must have deployed our men up to Glogova somewhere, but where exactly, I can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you inspect your men who were deployed along the road that night, did you review them?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Before leaving to get some rest that night, I inspected the men once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And would that be in addition to the occasion on which you actually deployed them?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, other than your 1st Company members, do you know whether there were any other special police or Jahorina members deployed along the road that night, the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the 2nd Company arrived, that moment is a bit hazy in my mind because I keep mixing -- confusing the two days, the 12th and the 13th. They blend in in my memory. I don't believe they came on the 12th. I think they were there on the 13th because we secured the same road on the 13th again, just broadening a bit the area we guarded. I don't know exactly when they arrived, and I must say I was also taken aback to see them. I couldn't understand what they were doing there. I'm not really sure when they arrived, but I know I was in contact with them on the 13th, and I'm not sure about the 12th.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay, sir. Do you remember discussing these two evenings and the deployed of the Jahorina members along the road with myself during your proofing sessions?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you also remember discussing these events with the investigators in your interview in 2000?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have a copy of that interview and a recording. I think that confused me a bit. I still believe that I was not in contact with them on the 12th, and I'm inclined to think that they were not even there on the 12th, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And just to be clear, sir, I'm referring to the evening of the 12th, when you had your men deployed approximately to Glogova. Okay? I'm not talking about what your recollection is in terms of the day of the 12th. I'm simply talking about the evening of the 12th and the evening of the 13th, just to make sure you understand that's the question I'm asking you. Okay? I want to ask you: Do you recall speaking and meeting with Mr. Ikonic at any time on the evening of the 12th?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you remember, sir, telling the investigators in 2000 and telling me during your proofing session that you met with Mr. Ikonic in Konjevic Polje on the evening of the 12th? Do you remember that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, but that's not what was written in the transcript, if my translation of that interview is correct. That really confused me a bit, because -- because that transcript made me think, and I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, sir, we'll get back to that perhaps after the break, but right now I want to move along a little bit, because I don't want to take up too much more time right now on this issue. Can you tell the Trial Chamber what happened on the 13th?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 13th, in the morning of the 13th, I was again given the assignment to go to Potocari because the transportation was not finished, and I went there again, this time with a smaller group of men, because most of my men had worked all night, and plus I was told there were not too many civilians left, so it was not a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what did you personally do that day, sir, in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was again on the location, doing the same job, but if I may be allowed to share one of my thoughts with you, I'd like to say that what happened on the 12th must have been pushed back into oblivion, and whenever I see something in the media that reminds me of it, the image that that brings up in my mind is the crowd, the people that I saw on the 12th, and there's nothing that happened on the 13th that stuck in my mind. The only thing I remember is that after the transports were over, we gathered close to the entrance to the UN base, waiting for our own vehicles to arrive, and then I saw a couple of those vehicles belonging to humanitarian organisations and I saw some people I knew from those humanitarian organisations. That's what I remember. But as for the final stages of the transportation, there is nothing special that I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And on the 13th, sir, did you still have your radio?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had a radio on me throughout the war, and I suppose I had it on the 13th as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you maintain radio contact with Mr. Jevic during the day of the 13th?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you have any recollection of seeing Mr. Jevic participating in the transportations on the 13th of July, sir?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, did you, yourself, participate in the separation of any Muslim men from their families on the 12th or 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Emphatically, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you see any separations of Muslim men from their families on the 12th or the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, certainly not. In the area where I was, standing right next to the civilians, certainly not.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you receive any reports of that happening on the 12th or 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody was either required to inform me, nor did anyone inform me. I received no information during those days.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you see any civilians abused, hit, kicked, or pushed towards or onto any of the buses on the 12th or 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for abuse of any kind in the location where I was standing with the people next to me, that didn't happen. It was not the most orderly transport, those were not tourist buses, that is true, but as for abuse, nobody abused anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, did you see any Muslim men directed towards or placed in any detention locations around the UN base on the 12th or 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you receive any information that that was happening on the 12th or 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you ever receive reports or information that any of your 1st Company members were seizing equipment such as vests and radios from Dutch soldiers on the 12th or 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the check-point, nobody seized anything from people by force or otherwise. Whether that happened elsewhere, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, sir, did you ever receive any information at any time that any of your 1st Company members or anyone from the Jahorina Training Centre or from the Special Police Brigade, for that matter, were seizing equipment such as vests and radios from Dutch soldiers on the 12th or 13th?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you receive any information, sir, that any of your 1st Company members disarmed or took weapons from any of the Dutch soldiers on the 12th or 13th?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you receive any information that any Special Police Brigade members, whether from the Jahorina Training Centre or elsewhere were doing that on the 12th or 13th?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you receive any information that any Special Police Brigade or Jahorina members detained or otherwise restricted the movement of any Dutch soldiers on either of those days?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall having contact or conversations with any VRS members on either of those days?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have contact with members of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So after these transportations ended on the 13th, what did you do, sir?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to our base. Back at the base, the usual procedure was followed; washing up, tidying up. I had a problem at the time that was very bad throughout the time I spent in Bratunac with that group of men. The first night on the 11th, when we just arrived at Bratunac, as I was waiting to be accommodated, two members of my unit asked me for permission to go and visit some family nearby because they were natives of that area. I didn't think twice before I allowed it, but they never came back. Another time, a group of seven or eight of them, and this is my assumption because I never investigated, escaped across the Drina to Serbia. While I was there, about a dozen members of my unit went absent without official leave, and I suppose they went to Serbia. That's what kept me busy for a while. Then late in the afternoon, it might have been evening already, Jevic came again and told me that we were to go to guard the road again, that the 2nd Company was there as well. I wondered what they were doing there, how come they arrived. The answer I got is that they had their own assignment, their own orders. And I then gathered a group of men who were fit enough to go - I can't remember the exact number - and we covered this time a long section of the road, and I believe that with one of those men whom I deployed, or perhaps it was one of the instructors who was with me, I looked at the slopes at the point where you enter Kravica, it's an area I knew from before, and we discussed where some kind of positions could be, and that's what helps me to remember that on that night we covered a longer section of the road. And from those earlier positions that we held in 1993, you have a very good vantage point. There are no trees obstructing the view to the road and it's easily recognisable.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, just to be absolutely clear, when exactly were you deployed to the Kravica area and in what capacity, previously?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Kravica area, you mean what I mentioned in 1993 or --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was an assignment that began in December 1992 and finished on the 7th of January, 1993. The dates are well known because it's the Orthodox Christmas on the 7th of January, and that's something that you don't forget. That's when I, with a group of people from my unit or a part of my unit from Bijeljina, because I was a commander of the detachment, I got there with the task of protecting the civilian population and helping in the operation to break through the Bratunac-Konjevic Polje road. I was there for some 10 or 12 days. Our assignment was, in a way, to offer some faith to those people that somebody is thinking of them, that something is happening there, in any case, while another main part of the members of the Army of Republika Srpska from the Bratunac direction tried to clear the road and to break through the blockade that was there. Do I need to explain what was happening?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No. Thank you, sir, I appreciate that. I just want to ask you: With respect to the features that you recognised in 1995 at Kravica, can you just describe, very briefly, what you did with respect to those features in 1992 to 1993, when you were there, just to give the Court some context how you recall this particular area? I think you described a hill, perhaps, from which you deployed some of your men.

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but this question is not quite clear to me. I need to explain the position in 1993; is that it? All right. It was a specific position from the aspect of some kind of combat concept because it's an elevation, there is a kind of elevation there and a kind of step where there are some houses. It's like a ridge. And at those houses, we made a kind of improvised line, and from that ridge we occasionally opened fire at the Muslim positions in order to attract attention so that a certain number of the Muslim forces would be drawn to us so that we would, to an extent, make it easier for the Bratunac forces to break through the blockade and clear the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And it's just this feature which is one of the features that you recognised in '95; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I recognised another place at the entrance of Kravica. It's a place, it's a hamlet. It's a part of the Kravica village named Djurici. This stuck in my mind, because my last name is Djuric, and for those reasons I remembered it. It's from the Bratunac direction as you enter Kravica. That's where it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how is it that on the night of the 13th you were able to deploy your men as far as Kravica, whereas the previous night you recall making it to Glogova only?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This time, too, we reached Glogova just before Kravica, but I recognised that part of Kravica and I know that I did comment on that. I don't know with whom. That part of Glogova is clear. You can see everything. There's just one curve on the road; everything else is clear. There are no woods, there are no hills. It's visible, It's a large, clear area, so the visibility is good.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I apologise, I asked an unclear question, sir. Let me just ask you this: On the night of the 13th, did you have more men available to you to deploy along that road, and if so, why?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that we did have more men available, because on the 13th, during the day, the Potocari engagement was very brief and there were no special other tasks, so we were able to engage a larger number of people on security. I think that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you inspect your men along the road on the evening of the 13th?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. I did come once or twice, perhaps even three times. I don't remember. But I did go, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And on the night of the 13th, do you remember making contact with Mr. Ikonic?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And would you describe that contact, please, with Mr. Ikonic?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went towards Konjevic Polje, and near the road by Konjevic Polje I met some members of our unit. I asked them, "Where is your superior officer?" Then they explained that they were billeted in some barracks near the road, near the intersection at Konjevic Polje. I went there and I met Major Nikolic [as interpreted] there. It was just a courtesy kind of conversation, friendly, without any explanations, what or how. "Major, what are you doing here?" "I don't know." So it was something like that. I didn't really discuss anything particular with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I believe that Mr. Thayer already noticed that the witness says, "There I met Major Nikolic" there on page 23, line 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And then again at line 8 there's a reference --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Major Ikonic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you for pointing that out. We observed that, too. The transcript will be corrected accordingly. Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, on the evening of the 13th, what was your understanding of the assignment that Mr. Ikonic's 2nd Company had with respect to securing the road?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I noticed that he was deploying his men in the same way that I was deploying mine, along the road, when I saw them, because Jevic told me that the other company had come and I was expecting them to do that. As to why he came, how he came, I don't know. He was a little bit confused. We didn't comment too much on that. I don't really remember if we discussed that in any particular way. It was just a cordial, collegial visit because we were both there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall communicating with Mr. Ikonic over the radio that evening?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I communicated with him the second time I met him. I think that we had contact over the communications system, over the radio then. I think that's how it was. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall where you met Mr. Ikonic the second time that evening?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where it was, but it was somewhere along the route where his men were deployed. I don't remember exactly where that was, and that part of the road away from Kravica is something that I'm really not very familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, is it your understanding, sir, that on the night of the 13th that your 1st Company and Mr. Ikonic's 1st Company were able to completely secure the entire road? And again that's Mr. Ikonic's 2nd Company and your 1st Company, sir? I think I misspoke a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we were not physically linked. I was probably receiving one order and Ikonic another. I don't know. I mean, I cannot state this with certainty. But I know that we were not linked and that in the second conversation, when I spoke with Nedjo, this is something that I do remember, that stuck in my mind, because there was nobody on the road. I said, "Well, it's strange that there's nobody there between us." He said, "Well, there's some troops up there above the road in the wooded area, but to tell you the truth, I really don't know."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the last part of that sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which troops, who was up there, he probably didn't know, either, so I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just to be clear, sir, when Mr. Ikonic was referring to troops, was he, first of all, referring to Serb troops or Muslim troops?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serb troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you know whether he was referring to MUP or Special Police Brigade troops or to regular VRS troops when he was making that reference to troops being --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It's a call for speculation. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm simply asking him whether he knows, based on his conversation, whether he was referring to MUP, Special Police Brigade or just regular VRS troops, if he knows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead. It's not speculation because it's based on his possible knowledge. If he is to speculate, then of course he knows that he shouldn't answer the question. But otherwise he should answer it.

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember him mentioning or saying that these were our members from the Police Brigade. Then he would probably know who it was and what, because he knows those people. He probably didn't know those people. He didn't tell me anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, I really -- I don't remember him saying that it was anyone, this person or that person. He said, "Some soldiers are up there, but I don't know which ones." I assume that had anyone from the Special Police Brigade been up there, he would have known about that. I assume so.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, on the nights of the 12th and 13th, were any Jahorina or Special Police Brigade or PJP members, to your knowledge, assigned to any guard duties in Bratunac, itself, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: None of my people had any other duties, other than protecting the road during the night. As for the others, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And were you aware that, for example, on the night of the 13th there were thousands of prisoners who were being held in and around the actual town of Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, at any time on the 12th or the 13th, did you receive any information of Muslims surrendering or being captured along that Bratunac-Konjevic Polje road?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: None of my soldiers told me anything, and when I was there I didn't notice anything. Therefore, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, do you recall whether you were actually on that road at any time during the day on the 12th or the 13th?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the Bratunac-Konjevic Polje road on the 12th or the 13th during the day, I was not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And were any of your 1st Company members deployed on that road during the day on the 12th or 13th, sir?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And on the evening of the 13th, is it your testimony that as far as you know, the only troops securing that Bratunac-Konjevic Polje road were your 1st Company members and Mr. Ikonic's 2nd Company members?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that we were and that Nedjo was there, but I cannot say with any degree of certainty if any others were doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, do you recall seeing any other troops along the road on the evening of the 12th or the 13th, performing the same duties that your 1st Company members were performing, sir?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the night of the 12th and the night of the 13th, that road, especially until midnight, was very busy. There was an exceptionally large number of vehicles passing, military police vehicles, civilian vehicles. I wasn't paying any attention to that because it was not my task to watch the traffic, but to protect the road or actually the area behind the road so that nobody would make an incursion onto the Bratunac road.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And that brings us to the 14th, sir. First of all, where did you spend the night of the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Other than those two visits, I spent most of that time at the base where the unit was billeted.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, can you tell the Trial Chamber what you did on the 14th of July?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot state it with 100 per cent degree of certainty, but I know that on that day, the 14th, we had no activities. We were down there at the school, and I know that I -- I assume that on the 14th, I went to Bijeljina to change, to take some fresh clothes, because everything that I was wearing was destroyed. And we had a problem. I and a large number of the unit members got some kind of rash, probably because of the bad hygiene and everything that was happening during those days.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So did you go to Potocari on the 14th, sir, at all?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall going to Bratunac for any specific reason on the 14th?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that if I went to Bijeljina on the 14th, that I had to pass through Bratunac, because the road passes. It's the only road.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: But do you recall having to conduct any business or have any specific reason to be in Bratunac on the 14th, other than passing through on your way to Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember having any assignment or business.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, on the 14th, sir, did you receive any information of anything in particular happening along the Bratunac-Konjevic Polje road the previous day?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you receive any information of Muslims surrendering or being captured along that road that day, the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember receiving any information.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, did you ever receive any information about an incident which occurred at the hangar in Kravica on the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Much later, I heard stories, gossip, all kinds of talk, but I think that that is not for me to bring before this Court. These are other people's stories. They can be true or not. In wars like this one of ours, there was many exhibitionists, boasts about some things. Some people admonish themselves, they wish they weren't in some place. It's all up to different people, how they take it. I heard something through the media, from what I can recall now, some questions, I think, it seems to me, the investigator put to me in 2000, and all of that is a mixture, so that I really don't know when I heard which information or what it was. More or less, I know from these stories later that something happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, when do you recall first hearing that anything unusual had happened at the hangar in Kravica?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Much, much later, after all of those events. I don't know, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Can you at least say whether it was a week, a month, six months, or a matter of years later that you first heard about anything unusual happening at the Kravica warehouse?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly. I know that more or less there was some kind of general story that some Serb soldiers were killed there, and then out of revolt, because of that killing, there was retribution, something like that. I really don't know what. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I see we're nearing the break. I have a couple of final areas to go into with this witness. If we may, can we break now and I might be able to streamline my final direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. Thayer. We'll have a 25-minute break starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before you continue and finish, Mr. Thayer, I refer you to the exhibits tendered and admitted with witness number 168. It was not a protected witness, Danko Gojkovic. It has been brought to my attention that out of the documents -- amongst the documents that we admitted as Prosecution exhibits, there are several that have not yet been translated from B/C/S into English. I'm going to list them very quickly. These will be marked for identification, as is the practice of this Trial Chamber, pending translation which is accepted by both parties, upon which then they will be upgraded to fully-admitted documents. This is P2778, 2779, 2782, 2781, 2782, 2783, 2784, 2787 and 2789. Okay, thank you. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and I'm advised that those documents have been submitted for translation, and we expect that shortly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning again, sir. Just a few more questions, and then I'll be concluding my examination. First, sir, I wanted to offer you an apology. I think I suggested, during my direct examination, that you had stated during your interview in 2000 that you had met with Mr. Ikonic on the night of 12th July, and I reviewed the transcript carefully and, in fact, you did not tell us that in 2000. I wanted to apologise. That was my error, and so I apologise for that and for any confusion that that created. I understand that perhaps our memories differ with respect to what you told me in the proofing session, but that's okay as well. Okay? Now, when you received this information, whenever it was, concerning what happened at the Kravica warehouse, did you make any inquiries or request any reports from any of your 1st Company members who had been deployed along the road on the 12th and the 13th?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't ask any reports from anybody. For a long time after those events in Bratunac and that area, I didn't stay long at the training centre; I had another assignment in Trnovo. And after that, I received new orders and went to join a unit in Doboj. So I left soon afterwards. And while I was in Bratunac, I didn't ask for any reports from anyone because I didn't even know what was going on, nor was I able to ask for any reports subsequently because I wasn't aware of what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you ever discuss the information that you received about the incident at the Kravica warehouse with Mr. Jevic?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My relationship with Mr. Jevic is a bit peculiar. We have not had any private communication since 1993, in fact since I was replaced in July 1992. If we communicated after that moment, it was purely officially, no private communication at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, my question, in fact, is: Did you have any official discussion with Mr. Jevic at any time about the information that you had received about what had happened at the Kravica hangar?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: How about with Mr. Borovcanin, did you ever have any official or unofficial discussion with Mr. Borovcanin at any time about what you had heard happened at the Kravica warehouse?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't talk to Mr. Borovcanin about it either.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, to the best of your recollection, where did you spend the evening of the 14th of July?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, I went to Bijeljina, but whether I returned the same day, that evening or the next day in the morning, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you say "returned," sir, are you meaning returned to the Jahorina Training Centre?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That whole time, 14th, the 15th, is completely gone from my memory. The only thing that I remember about that time is our return to Jahorina and that I was engaged up there to organise for the members of my unit, whose physical condition and clothing was in a terrible state, a spraying against allergy and hygienic treatment, because they were suffering from skin conditions. That's the only thing I remember. I don't remember anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay, sir. May we have P02478 displayed on e-court, please. This is a colour aerial shot, so it may take a little bit of time to upload. And while we're waiting for it to upload, sir, I just want you to think about, first of all, where you were spending your time on the 12th and 13th, and see if you can locate that position on this map. Just take your time, orient yourself to this photograph, and I want you first to see if you can identify the general area where you were working on the 12th and 13th of July. And with Madam Usher's assistance, I'm going to ask you to circle that area. First, I just want to ask you, do you see that area where you were working on the 12th and 13th?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this area, in this locality, I had never been before or after. The only thing I remember are these trees here and this area around the trees. It's the only indication that helps me remember where exactly we were, and I know I deployed my men up to here factory, up to this factory here, and I remember people standing on this plateau, looking for shade. I remember that I was here. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you've drawn a narrow, oval shape, and just so I'm clear, you're indicating where you recall you were working on the 12th and the 13th by that circle, by that oval?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on the road. That's where they were moving.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Underneath that little oval, sir, would you just write your initials?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here? Can I do it here? [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That's good enough, sir, thank you. And you indicated that some of your soldiers had been deployed in the area, I think, of a factory. Can you just indicate that location with an "X"?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My soldiers were deployed around the civilians, and depending on how the civilians moved, in which area they filled, my men adjusted their position. There was no strictly-defined guard post. And I think, to the best of my recollection, this is the structure. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you've indicated that with three dots and then an "X." Now, the last question I have for you, sir, with this overhead, is: Can you please mark with an arrow the direction you took when you entered Potocari on the morning of the 12th? Okay. You've drawn two arrows. The lower arrow, I take it, is to depict the route that you personally took; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I personally took the road, and a number of my men went on the left and on the right side of the road, whereas another group went behind this factory or whatever it is, this base here. I remember there was a little river there. That's how they went. And when I was somewhere at the beginning, the soldiers from here told me that they had seen a couple of burned houses with smoke still coming from these houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And when you refer to the soldiers "from here," sir, you're referring to the soldiers represented by the upper arrow who travelled around the UN base; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the members of the unit that I led.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, finally, sir, would you just, under the lower arrow that denotes your movement, would you just place your initials and "12 July," please?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And above the upper arrow, if you would just write "1st Company."

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The lower arrow is also the 1st Company. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And if you would -- I see my friend --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I would like to assist the Trial Chamber and my colleague, because this might cause a confusion if it's written "1st Company," because there was also the 1st Company of PJP and the 1st Company from Jahorina. If he could just add "Jahorina Centre", just to make it sure that everything is clear on these markings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that's a very wise suggestion, Mr. Thayer, if you could follow it. He needs to tell us what he has written.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wrote again "Company," but it's not necessary because it's already written. I should write "Training Centre, Jahorina."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And if you would just place your initials and today's date - it's the 2nd of May - in the upper right-hand corner, and then we'll be done with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he has already put his initials at the bottom of that page, in the center.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I mean, abundance is always a good thing to have.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Madam Usher. I think we can save the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Not on this document, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, I just want to show you a very brief video clip that you were shown in 2000 and again during our proofing session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you require sound or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'm just looking to see if people -- we're not receiving sound. I don't think it's necessary to have sound, Mr. President, but if my friends do, then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyone wishes to be able to hear the sound? Any of the accused? Okay, go ahead. I think we can live without it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, pausing at 2.25.45.08, do you recognise anyone in this frame?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. That's the officer of the UN with whom, on that day, the 12th, and the next day, 13th, I worked together guarding the civilians. That's the one I described as a tall, blonde, well-built young man.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And he's --

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lieutenant, if his name is van Duijn, then I got it right. But I'm not sure about the name. It doesn't mean anything to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And would you just identify an article of clothing that he's wearing, for the record?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's wearing the blue UN cap, a T-shirt.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine, sir, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, we've frozen at 2.26.14.06. Do you recognise the individual in the middle of this frame wearing the blue vest?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see in this image that that is the man who interpreted for us. I suppose that it's one of the men from my unit who helped us with interpretation, because I had no specific duties concerning liaison with the UN, so I wasn't supplied with an interpreter beforehand. This was an arrangement made on the spot. He is a bit unusually dressed, and even his blue bulletproof vest is a bit unusual. I suppose that's him. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall this individual's name or nickname, by any chance?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw it on the subtitles, but you also reminded me. Miki is a nickname I knew him by, but it doesn't mean anything specific to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So is it fair to say, sir, that you don't have an independent recollection, as you sit here today, as to what this interpreter's name was?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't. I don't remember the names of any of the members of my unit. I spent only a few days with those men, and I didn't memorise their names. And as for the faces, it was a long time ago. I really don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recognise who the individual is at the far left of this frame?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I recognise myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, we've stopped the video at 2.26.54.07. When we reviewed this video clip in my office, you pointed out something about an individual in this frame. Can you just share that with the Trial Chamber, please?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we were talking, I noticed that this was a member of my unit on the left, and there were UN members on the right-hand side. Wherever their men were, there were some of my men, so all the time there was cooperation between us, although it didn't follow any strict orders. It was a natural arrangement that just happened on the ground. Maybe some people would have something to say about the cigarette in this man's mouth, but considering the way he joined the unit, I'm not surprised, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Finally, sir, do you recognise anyone in this frame at 2.27.53.09?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a bit unclear, but I believe that's Mr. Ljubomir Borovcanin, the one on the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, we've advanced it to 2.27.55.09. Does that help you any with the certainty of your identification?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's easier, and I also see the insignia of his brigade on his arm. Yes, that's Mr. Ljubomir Borovcanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you say "his brigade," what are you referring to, sir?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean the Special Brigade of the Police of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just a couple of final questions, sir. Did you discipline any of your Jahorina Training Facility members in connection with their deployment to Potocari and the Bratunac-Konjevic Polje road in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I had no information that they had done anything that would merit any sort of measures against them, I didn't take any steps. And as for Potocari, I think that would have been absurd.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And are you aware, sir, of any investigation being initiated by the Special Police Brigade or by the RS MUP following the deployment of the Special Police Brigade forces to those areas, Potocari and the Bratunac-Konjevic Polje road in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that period when all that was happening, I was an officer who had been replaced. I was not with the command of the brigade or the command of the detachment. I was an instructor, and I had no access to information that would tell me whether something had been initiated or not. I don't know. I can't say anything one way or another because I was not part of a combat unit as an officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Jevic ever ask you for any report concerning the actions of the Jahorina or Special Police Brigade members in Potocari and along the road in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no report was required of me, and I didn't write anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Borovcanin ever ask you for any such report?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did anyone, sir?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one, ever. The only contact I had with the Ministry of the Interior was when I gave a statement to the commission established to investigate the events in Srebrenica. That's when I was in contact with the MUP, and I gave them my statement to the OTP investigators from 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And this commission is what's commonly known as the RS Commission; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Commission of Republika Srpska for inquiry into events of Srebrenica and the area of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just to be clear, did you provide any statement to the RS Commission, other than providing your 2000 interview with the OTP?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't give any particular report to the police. I just gave them a transcript of my interview with the investigators from 2000. And I had another contact with somebody concerning this case when the Defence team of Mr. Blagojevic, I believe, asked some clarification from me regarding the statement I had given, and I believe it was certified by an official of the Tribunal. I remember signing every page. So I provided that addendum, and that's all the communication I had in this connection.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And from your understanding, sir, the statement that you gave to the Blagojevic Defence team, along with your OTP statement from 2000, became some type of evidence in that trial, but you didn't have to testify; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I have no further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Thayer. Now, let's review a little bit the position from the Defence side. I have the Borovcanin Defence team that have asked for two and a half hours. Yes, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I believe I'll stick to my estimation. It could be a bit less, maybe a bit more, but that's a rough estimation. I think it's going to be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the Beara and Miletic teams have asked for 45 minutes each. Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. It will probably be a little less than that, probably closer to 30 minutes, if at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Ms. Fauveau has, for the record, nodded. Actually, is it 45 or 10 minutes, Madame Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's been a mistake, unfortunately. I will need 45 minutes rather than 10 minutes, but it depends on the questions put by the other Defence counsel. Then it could not perhaps take as long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Zivanovic, you requested 20 minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, and I stick to my estimate at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And, Mr. Haynes, you requested a quarter of an hour?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: We'll have no questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So let's -- I suppose it would be better if you start, Mr. Lazarevic, unless there is an arrangement -- a different arrangement. Okay, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. I'm going to start.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Good day, sir. I am a lawyer, Aleksandar Lazarevic. I am defending Mr. Borovcanin, and I'm going to put certain questions to you about your testimony before this Tribunal. First of all, I would like to clarify certain facts relating to your statement to the Prosecutor and the Defence of Colonel Blagojevic. Mr. Karnavas also asked you about that, except other than the testimony today and yesterday and these statements that you gave to the investigators from the Prosecutor's office, and the statement you gave to Mr. Blagojevic's Defence attorney, which was a clarification of certain details from your statement, you practically did not provide any other statements either to the bodies of the Tribunal or the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina or Republika Srpska; you didn't provide any statements to any state organs?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave a statement to the Ministry of Internal Affairs. However, there was probably a replacement in the Commission because they called me again, and it was the same thing. I didn't give another statement, but they summoned me twice. I didn't give any statement in particular, I mean, except once, which I was requested to do, and I did this in written form.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: To clarify, because of the existence of certain written documents which could have some relation to the further course of these proceedings, you handed them over your statement; you didn't say anything more about these events?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't talk about the events with them. I just handed them over a copy of the conversation or interview I had in 2002 with the investigators in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That clarifies things to quite a significant degree. At the beginning, I would just like to put several questions to you in order to clarify to the Trial Chamber the status and the structure of the Jahorina Training Centre, and I think you are the exact witness who could help us in that. In your interview with the investigators of The Hague Tribunal, this is in October of 2000, on page 15 of your statement, or page 20 of your statement in English, you said that the Jahorina Centre had about 100 people in training. These were deserters who had been brought from Yugoslavia, and they were mostly deployed in the Army of Republika Srpska while a smaller number to the Ministry of Internal Affairs. This part of your statement, did I understand you correctly if I say that these people who were assigned to the -- or these deserters who were sent for training to the Ministry of Internal Affairs of Republika Srpska were actually the people who were from the Jahorina Centre who were there for training?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When -- well, Mr. Jevic told me when these people were being brought from Serbia, depending on the age of the persons and probably some other elements that I'm not aware of because I wasn't there, I wasn't assigning these people, but, anyway, these were sort of younger people who could go through that kind of training with us, they were assigned to the Ministry of Internal Affairs, and most of those people who had been rounded up went to the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: When you say "rounded up," I assume that these were conscripts who had fled Republika Srpska, trying to avoid the war.

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the several days of training that we had and the time we spent together, I listened to some stories of the experiences of those people. There are some people who had left Serbia before the war, who left immediately prior to the war, and there were those who actually left only a couple of months before they were actually arrested over there. So there were classic deserters there and there were others who perhaps could not be described in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The Jahorina Centre where you were a trainer was founded by the Republika Srpska Ministry of Internal Affairs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And it belonged to the MUP of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By the logic of things, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: However, in order to separate things here, the people who carried out the training, who conducted the training, people like yourself and other instructors, they belonged to the Brigade of the Special Police?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, except for two.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, but your answer is not in the transcript or the transcript is blocked. Oh, it's all right now. Now, precisely, in relation to those people who were there for not members of that Brigade of Special Police and they took part in the training at Jahorina, these were therefore inspectors of the RS MUP and they were also trainers from the School for Internal Affairs in Banja Luka; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: So if I were to define the centre as an organisational unit of the MUP in which the Special Police Brigade had certain tasks, would that be a correct definition?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that -- I don't know the definition. I cannot really follow it quite precisely, but in essence the Police Brigade, that organisational part, and then the other part is the training part.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: All right. I think that that is precisely what I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, but I just can't follow the definition in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: If, for a minute, we now go back to your interview with The Hague Tribunal Prosecutor's Office, this is page 25, lines 13 to 15, or rather on page 32 of the English version, speaking about the attendees that you described as deserters, you said, speaking about them, that this was not a special unit, I'm quoting you, and that it had nothing to do with the special unit. And then continuing with your description, you said that it was a group of people, some of whom -- actually, who were trained by a number of people, who were not special operations people. Further on the same page in line 25, you say, "It's absurd to put deserters and special policemen on the same level." Do you recall saying that?
